question_text: Traumatic, acceleration/deceleration injuries to the aorta usually occur where its mobile and fixed portions meet. This would be at the:
explanation:
The ligamentum arteriosum is the point where the left pulmonary artery connects with the undersurface of aortic arch. It is a remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, which shunted blood away from the developing lungs. Because the aorta is tethered to the pulmonary artery by the ligamentum arteriosum, the part of the aorta near the ligamentum is vulnerable to damage in a traumatic acceleration/deceleration injury - it could pull away and tear. The other answer choices do not describe points of the aorta where a mobile and fixed portion meet. Therefore, these parts of the aorta would not be vulnerable to this type of traumatic injury.

question_text: In Angina pectoris, which nerve is involved in radiation of chest pain to the left arm?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The T2 dermatome corresponds to the upper medial arm, axilla, and some part of the upper chest.
  • The intercostobrachial nerve is the lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve (T2), carries the referred pain to the medial side of the left arm
  • This, explains the characteristic chest pain radiating to the arm in anghina pectoris.

question_text: A stethoscope placed over the left second intercostal space just lateral to the sternum would be best positioned to detect sounds associated with which heart valve?
explanation:
The best place to listen to heart valves is not at their actual sternocostal projections. If you place your stethoscope exactly where a valve is located, you may not hear anything because the valve might be deep in the chest or the sound might be muffled by bone or cartilage. Instead, you want to listen to the valves by putting your stethescope at a point downstream from the valve where you can hear the blood flowing and colliding with the muscular chest wall.

There are points of auscultation for all four heart valves: Pulmonic: left second intercostal space, lateral to the sternal angle; Aortic: right second intercostal space, lateral to the sternal angle; Mitral: left fifth intercostal space, 8cm away from the midline; Tricuspid: left fourth intercostal space, just lateral to the sternum.

question_text: ADH acts on which of the following sites of the nephron?
explanation:
Explanation:

Medullary collecting duct is the main site of ADH action in the nephron.

ADH binds to V2 receptors on principal cells, triggering insertion of aquaporin-2 channels, allowing water to be reabsorbed into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium.

The medullary region has a steep osmotic gradient maintained by the countercurrent mechanism, which allows maximal concentration of urine under the influence of ADH.

Explanation of Other Options:

PCT (Option A)

The PCT reabsorbs about 65-70% of filtered water and solutes, but this water reabsorption is not under the influence of ADH.

The water permeability in the PCT is always high, regardless of the body's hydration status - it is not regulated hormonally.

Cortical CD (Option B)

ADH does act on the entire collecting duct system, including the cortical portion, but the maximal effect is seen in the medullary part.

The osmotic gradient for water reabsorption is more significant in the medullary interstitium, so that's where ADH has the most potent effect.

DCT (Option C)

The early DCT is impermeable to water, regardless of ADH levels.

Water reabsorption does not occur here, and ADH has no significant effect in this segment.

The early DCT is more involved in Na⁺ and Cl⁻ reabsorption via the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter.

Key Takeaways:

ADH acts primarily on the medullary portion of the collecting duct to regulate water reabsorption. The osmotic gradient in the medulla is essential for the effectiveness of ADH in concentrating urine.

question_text: Which electrolyte abnormality will lead to cardiac arrhythmia in a patient with severe vomiting?
explanation:
Explanation:

Severe vomiting leads to significant loss of gastric fluid, which is rich in hydrochloric acid and potassium, resulting in hypokalemia. Hypokalemia prolongs repolarisation, making myocardial cells more excitable and prone to developing abnormal electrical activity, which manifests as various cardiac arrhythmias

Explanation of Other Options:

Hyperkalemia (Option B): While hyperkalemia also causes severe cardiac arrhythmias and can be life-threatening, it is typically not seen in severe vomiting, which mainly causes potassium loss, leading to hypokalemia.

Hyponatremia (Option C): Severe vomiting can lead to hyponatremia and cause neurological symptoms (e.g., seizures, altered mental status) and cerebral edema. It is not directly associated with cardiac arrhythmias as a primary mechanism compared to potassium abnormalities.

Hypocalcemia (Option D): Severe hypocalcemia can prolong the QT interval on an ECG and predispose to Torsades de Pointes; it is not a primary electrolyte abnormality in acute vomiting, causing arrhythmia when compared to hypokalemia.

Key Takeaway: Severe vomiting most commonly causes hypokalemia due to gastric potassium loss, directly impairing cardiac myocyte repolarisation and significantly increasing the risk of life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.

question_text: A needle inserted into the 9th intercostal space along the midaxillary line would enter which space?
explanation:
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest extent of the pleural cavity or sac. It is the part of the pleural sac where the costal pleura changes into the diaphragmatic pleura. It is also the area into which a needle is inserted for thoracocentesis, and it is found at different levels at different areas of the thorax. At the mid clavicular line, the costodiaphragmatic recess is between ribs 6 and 8; at the midaxillary line it is between 8 and 10; and at the paravertebral line it is between 10 and 12. So, inserting the needle just above the 9th rib at the midaxillary line should put you in the costodiaphragmatic recess.

question_text: The internal thoracic artery is sometimes surgically cut near the caudal end of the sternum and used to supply blood to a region of the heart. In these cases, maintenance of adequate blood flow to the rectus abdominis may be dependent on increased flow through which artery?
explanation:
If the internal thoracic artery was ligated, blood would no longer flow to the superior epigastric artery, which is the branch of the internal thoracic that supplies blood to rectus abdominis. However, the superior epigastric artery communicates with the inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery. This means that blood could flow from the external iliac, to the inferior epigastric, to the superior epigastric and the rectus abdominis. The superficial epigastric and superficial circumflex iliac arteries are two superficial branches of the femoral artery. They do not supply deep structures in the abdomen. The distal portions of the umbilical arteries are obliterated in adults--they are the medial umbilical ligaments that form the medial umbilical folds. The deep circumflex iliac artery courses along the iliac crest on the inner surface of the abdominal wall. It is too lateral to supply blood to rectus abdominis.

The aortic hiatus is not in the central tendon of the diaphragm--the caval opening, for the inferior vena cava, is found in the central tendon of the diaphragm. The aortic hiatus is formed by the median arcuate ligament, which unites the two crura of the diaphragm. The vertebrocostal trigone is an area of the diaphragm superior to the lateral arcuate ligament. Here, the diaphragmatic muscle is deficient and the trigone is closed primarily by the inferior and superior fascia of the diaphragm. It is a significant area for hernias. The esophageal hiatus is formed entirely by the fibers of the right crus. The psoas major muscle passes behind the medial arcuate ligament. Finally, the right phrenic nerve passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm, near the vena caval foramen. See Netter Plate 181 for a picture of all these structures and their relationships.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Abdomen, Page number - 185

question_text: Regarding the neurovascular bundle within the typical intercostal space, which of the following statements is FALSE?
option_a: The intercostal nerve lies between the external intercostal and internal intercostal muscles
option_b: Derivatives from T7 to T11 supply the anterior abdominal wall
option_c: T4 and T5 intercostal nerves are typical in type
option_d: The intercostal nerve is located inferior to the intercostal artery (VAN order)
explanation:
The structure marked A is the intercostal nerve.

It doesn't lie between external and internal intercostal muscles, but lies between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.

Typical intercostal nerves are those that only supply only the thoracic wall, e.g, 3rd to 6th intercostal nerves.

question_text: A cancerous growth from the body of the 9th thoracic vertebra exerts pressure anterolaterally. Which structure lies in direct contact with this growth?
explanation:
The thoracic splanchnic nerves lie on the anterior surfaces of the vertebral bodies. Remember, the splanchnic nerves lie medial to the sympathetic trunk, which is lying on the heads of the ribs. The vagus nerve lies in the anterior chest and eventually forms the esophageal plexus, covering the esophagus. The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm--it is not near the posterior wall of the thorax. Intercostal nerves run in the intercostal groove at the posterior border of the rib--they are not near the vertebral bodies.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 162

question_text: Which of the following is true about the left phrenic nerve?
option_a: Arise from dorsal rami of C2, C3, and C4
option_b: Descends in the left pleural space
option_c: Supplies the parietal peritoneum on the diaphragm
option_d: Passes through the vena caval opening in the diaphragm
explanation:
The left phrenic nerve supplies sensory fibers to the parietal peritoneum covering the diaphragm, and the mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleura on the left side.

The phrenic nerve is a mixed nerve derived mostly from the C4 ramus and also receives contributions from the C3 and C5 ventral rami. It is formed at the lateral border of scalenus anterior.

The phrenic nerve is a mixed nerve derived mostly from the C4 ramus and also receives contributions from the C3 and C5 ventral rami. It is formed at the lateral border of scalenus anterior.

It descends anterior to the pulmonary hilum and lies between the mediastinal pleura and fibrous pericardium. It passes through the muscular part of the diaphragm just anterior to the central tendon. The right phrenic nerve passes through the vena caval opening.

Both right and left phrenic nerves supply:

  • Motor fibers to the muscular diaphragm - respective crura of the diaphragm
  • Sensory fibers to the mediastinal pleura, fibrous and serous pericardium, and diaphragmatic peritoneum.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 162

question_text: The neurovascular bundle in the thoracic wall is located between:
explanation:
Explanation:

The intercostal neurovascular bundle (Vein - Artery - Nerve) lies in the costal groove on the inferior border of each rib. Its precise location is: Between the internal intercostal muscle and the innermost intercostal muscle (intercostalis intimi)

Layers of the thoracic wall (external to internal):

  1. Skin
  2. Superficial fascia
  3. External intercostal muscle
  4. Internal intercostal muscle
  5. Intercostal neurovascular bundle (VAN)
  6. Innermost intercostal muscle (intercostalis intimi)
  7. Endothoracic fascia
  8. Parietal pleura

The VAN bundle runs in the intercostal space, protected by the rib's costal groove, and is clinically important for procedures such as intercostal nerve blocks and chest tube insertion.

Key Takeaways: -

The neurovascular bundle is arranged in the following order from above downwards: (Mnemonic: VAN )

  • Intercostal Vein
  • Intercostal Artery
  • Intercostal Nerve

question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect for the external intercostal muscle?
option_a: It extends from lateral border of sternum to angle of ribs
option_b: It arises from the lower border of rib above the space
option_c: It is inserted on the outer lip of the upper border of rib below
option_d: The direction of fibers is downward, forward and medially
explanation:
Explanation:

External intercostal muscles do not extend up to the sternum. They begin at the tubercles of the ribs posteriorly and end near the costochondral junction anteriorly. From this point to the sternum, the muscle is replaced by the external intercostal membrane.

External Intercostal Muscles:

  • Occupy the outermost intercostal space
  • Run from rib tubercle (posteriorly) to costochondral junction (anteriorly)
  • Beyond this, replaced by a thin membrane
  • Origin: Lower border of rib above (Option B)
  • Insertion: Outer lip of upper border of rib below (Option C)
  • Fiber direction: Downward, forward, and medially (like putting hands in pockets) (Option D)
  • Function: Elevation of ribs during inspiration

question_text: All of the following are tributaries of the marked vein except:
explanation:
Explanation:

The marked vein is the Azygos vein. The 5th to 11th left posterior intercostal veins drain into the hemiazygos or accessory hemiazygos veins, not directly into the azygos vein.

Azygos Vein

  • Drains the thoracic wall and upper lumbar region.
  • Forms an important collateral channel between the superior and inferior vena cava.

Formation

Formed by the union of:

  • Right subcostal vein
  • Right ascending lumbar vein
  • Lumbar azygos vein (variable contribution)

Course

  • Enters the thorax through the aortic opening (hiatus) of the diaphragm.
  • Ascends along the right side of the vertebral column.
  • At the level of T4, arches anteriorly over the root of the right lung.
  • Terminates by draining into the superior vena cava.

Tributaries

  • Right superior intercostal vein (Option A)
  • 5th to 11th right posterior intercostal veins
  • Hemiazygos vein (Option D)
  • Accessory hemiazygos vein
  • Right bronchial vein (Option C)
  • Several oesophageal, mediastinal, and pericardial veins

question_text: Which of the following match is correct for parts of Parietal pleura as shown in the given image ?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pleura is a serous membrane lined by mesothelium and forms two pleural sacs, one on each side of the mediastinum.
Each sac is invaginated from the medial side by the lung, creating two layers:

  • Parietal pleura (outer layer)
  • Visceral or pulmonary pleura (inner layer)

Visceral (Pulmonary) Pleura:

  • Covers the entire lung surface and lung fissures except at the hilum
  • Firmly adherent to lung tissue
  • Cannot be separated from lung
  • Nerve supply: Autonomic
    • Sympathetic: T2 to T5
    • Parasympathetic: Vagus nerve

Parietal Pleura:

Supplied by intercostal nerves (peripheral parts) and phrenic nerve (central diaphragm and mediastinum).
It has four distinct parts:

  • Cervical pleura:
    • Covers the apex of the lung
    • Projects above the first rib into the root of the neck
  • Costal pleura:
    • Lines the inner surface of thoracic wall, ribs, and intercostal spaces
  • Mediastinal pleura:
    • Covers the mediastinum and forms the lateral boundary of the mediastinal space
  • Diaphragmatic pleura:
    • Covers the superior surface of the diaphragm

question_text: A twenty-year-old woman was broad-sided on the driver side by an SUV and was taken to the hospital emergency room. Examination showed low blood pressure and tenderness on the left mid-axillary line. Also, a large swelling was felt protruding downward and medially below the left costal margin. X-rays revealed that her 9th and 10th ribs were fractured near their angles on the left side. The abdominal organ most likely to be injured by the fracture is:
explanation:
The spleen is usually well protected by the 9th through 12th ribs on the left side. But, if one or more of these ribs gets fractured, the spleen is the first organ to be ruptured. The spleen can also be damaged if there is blunt trauma to the abdomen or a sudden increase in intraabdominal pressure. This patient has several symptoms of a ruptured spleen--she has tenderness on the left posterior axillary line and hypotension. (Because of its spongy parenchyma and thin capsule, a ruptured spleen will bleed profusely and a patient may become hypotensive.) The stomach, splenic flexure of the colon, tail of the pancreas, left kidney, and suprarenal gland are in the same quadrant of the abdomen, and they are also at risk for injury. But, you should remember that the spleen is at greatest risk because of its close relationship with the 9th through 12th ribs.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Abdomen, Page number - 159

question_text: Which of the following correctly represents the structures related to the neck of the 1st rib from medial to lateral?
option_a: Sympathetic chain - Posterior intercostal vein - Superior intercostal artery - 1st thoracic nerve
option_b: 1st thoracic nerve - Superior intercostal artery - Posterior intercostal vein - Sympathetic chain
option_c: Posterior intercostal artery - Posterior intercostal vein - Sympathetic chain - 1st thoracic nerve
option_d: Posterior intercostal vein - Superior intercostal artery - 1st thoracic nerve - Sympathetic chain
explanation:
Explanation:

From medial to lateral, the structures related to the neck of the 1st rib are:

  • Sympathetic chain (most medial)
  • Posterior intercostal vein
  • Superior intercostal artery
  • 1st thoracic nerve (most lateral)

This sequence reflects the typical neurovascular arrangement around the neck of the 1st rib.

The neck of the 1st rib serves as an important landmark for understanding the relationships of thoracic neurovascular structures.

  • Medial structures: The sympathetic chain runs vertically, closely related to the vertebral bodies.
  • Vascular structures: The posterior intercostal vein lies anterior to the artery at this level as it drains into the azygos system.
  • Arterial structure: The superior intercostal artery supplies the first two intercostal spaces and lies lateral to the vein.
  • Nerve: The 1st thoracic nerve exits laterally and lies furthest from the midline among this group.

Key take aways :

The neck of 1st rib related medial to lateral side to : (Mnemonics : Chain pulling VAN)

  • Sympathetic Chain
  • Posterior intercostal Vein
  • Superior intercostal Artery
  • 1st thoracic Nerve

question_text: The image shows the cross-section of the abdominal cavity. Identify the structure marked 'A.'
explanation:
Explanation:

In a typical axial cross-section of the abdomen, the descending (abdominal) aorta is positioned anterior to the vertebral body and slightly to the left. It is the main arterial trunk supplying the abdominal viscera and walls via its major branches (celiac trunk, SMA, IMA, renal arteries).

Explanation of other options:

Superior vena cava (Option B): This large vein is located in the superior mediastinum, draining blood from the upper body into the right atrium; it is not present in the abdominal cavity.

Inferior vena cava (Option C): The IVC is a large vein that lies anterior to the vertebral column and to the right of the abdominal aorta, which is not the described position.

Ascending aorta (Option D): This part of the aorta is located in the thorax, ascending from the left ventricle before arching posteriorly.

Key Takeaways:

  • The abdominal aorta is anterior to the spine and slightly left of the midline.
  • It gives off major branches to supply the abdomen.

question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with choking episodes after ingestion of a fish bone while eating. X-ray shows that the fish bone is impacted at the level of T4 in the oesophagus. Which of the following is the most likely site of obstruction?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The oesophagus has four natural constrictions where foreign bodies commonly get impacted. These are at:
    1. Cricopharyngeal junction (15 cm from incisors; C6 level)
    2. Arch of the aorta (25 cm from incisors; T4 level)
    3. Left main bronchus (27 cm from incisors; T5 level)
    4. Oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm (40 cm from incisors; T10 level)
  • In this patient, the fish bone is stuck at T4, which corresponds to the arch of the aorta crossing the oesophagus. Hence, the correct answer is the arch of the aorta.

Explanation of other options:

Cricopharynx (Option A): This is the narrowest part of the oesophagus at the upper end (C6), but it is not at T4.

Left bronchus (Option C): Causes another constriction, but at the level of T5, not T4.

Diaphragm (Option D): Constriction at the oesophageal hiatus occurs at T10, much lower than the site of impaction in this case.

question_text: A 78-year-old female presented with edema of the left upper limb due to poor venous return. Examination revealed an aneurysm of the ascending aorta that was impinging on a large vein lying immediately anterosuperior to it, most likely the:
explanation:
Remember that the ascending aorta is the short part of the aorta emerging from the heart before the aortic arch. The left brachiocephalic vein is the only vein listed which is anterosuperior to that part of the aorta. It crosses horizontally through the mediastinum to join with the right brachiocephalic vein and form the superior vena cava. The right brachiocephalic vein stays on the right side of the chest and would not be affected by the aortic aneurysm. The azygos vein is also on the right side of the chest, and it lays deep in the thoracic cavity. The internal thoracic vein lies on the interior surface of the anterior wall of the chest. Although it drains into the brachiocephalic vein, it would not be affected by the aneurysm. The left superior intercostal vein crosses the aortic arch laterally, but its blockage would only affect drainage of intercostal spaces 2-4 on the left side.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 127

question_text: All of the following are constrictions of the oesophagus except:

  • Thoracic (aortic) constriction

  • Bronchial constriction
    • Where it is crossed by left main bronchus (T5) (Option B)
  • Diaphragmatic constriction
    • Where it passes through diaphragm at T10 (Option C)

Key takeaways :

The oesophagus shows 4 constrictions:

  • At its beginning, crossed by cricopharyngeus. 15 cm from the incisor teeth
  • Crossed byaortic arch, 22.5 cm from incisor teeth
  • Crossed by left bronchus, 27.5 cm from incisor teeth
  • Pierces the diaphragm, 37.5 cm from incisor teeth

question_text: All of the following structure are present at marked body surface landmark except
option_a: Arch of aorta begins and ends at this level
option_b: Azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung to end in superior vena cava
option_c: Intervertebral disc between T5 and T6
option_d: Trachea bifurcates into right and left principal bronchi
explanation:
Explanation:

The marked landmark is the Sternal Angle. The sternal angle corresponds to the intervertebral disc between T4 and T5, not T5 and T6.

The sternal angle (Angle of Louis) is a key anatomical landmark at the junction between the manubrium and sternum. It corresponds to:

  • Second costal cartilage articulates with the sternum - important for rib counting
  • Corresponds to the intervertebral disc between T4 and T5
  • Marks the division between superior and inferior mediastinum
  • Ascending aorta ends at this level
  • Arch of aorta begins and ends at this level (Option A)
  • Descending aorta begins at this level
  • Trachea bifurcates into right and left principal bronchi (Option D)
  • Pulmonary trunk divides into right and left pulmonary arteries
  • Upper border of the heart lies at this level
  • Azygos vein arch passes over the right lung root to drain into the SVC (Option B)

Key takeaways:

The sternal angle is a key landmark for the second costal cartilage, T4-T5 intervertebral disc, beginning of the descending aorta, bifurcation of the trachea, division of the pulmonary trunk, upper border of the heart, and the arch of the azygos vein into the superior vena cava.

question_text: The sternal angle is a landmark for locating the level of the:
explanation:
The sternal angle is a very important anatomical landmark which is used when placing the stethoscope and listening for heart sounds. The sternal angle is the location of the attachment of the costal cartilage of the second rib to the sternum. So, once you locate the sternal angle on a patient, you know the location of the second rib, and you can use that landmark to find the right spots to auscultate each valve of the heart. Also remember that a horizontal plane through the sternal angle passes through the T4/T5 intervertebral disc and marks the inferior boundary of the superior mediastinum. 

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 127

question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect for posterior intercostal arteries?
option_a: There are eleven posterior intercostal arteries on each side
option_b: The left posterior intercostal arteries are longer than right
option_c: 3rd to 11th posterior intercostal arteries arise from descending thoracic aorta
option_d: Posterior intercostal artery ends by anastomosing with upper anterior intercostal artery of space
explanation:
Explanation:

The right posterior intercostal arteries must travel farther, crossing behind the oesophagus, thoracic duct, azygos vein, and sympathetic chain.

Posterior Intercostal Arteries:

  • Number: There are 11 posterior intercostal arteries on each side, one in each intercostal space from 3rd to 11th (the 12th is the subcostal artery). (Option A)
  • Origin:
    • 1st and 2nd posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery (branch of costocervical trunk).
    • 3rd to 11th posterior intercostal arteries arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta. (Option C)
  • Side Differences:
    • The aorta lies on the left side of the vertebral column.
    • Right posterior intercostal arteries are longer (traveling farther across). Left posterior intercostal arteries are shorter. (Option B)
  • Course:
    • Right posterior intercostal arteries pass behind the:
      • Oesophagus
      • Thoracic duct
      • Azygos vein
      • Sympathetic chain
    • Left posterior intercostal arteries pass behind the:
      • Hemiazygos vein
      • Sympathetic chain
  • Termination: Each posterior intercostal artery ends near the costochondral junction, where it anastomoses with the upper anterior intercostal artery of the same space.

question_text: A patient who is chronic smoker presented with cough, chest pain, dyspnea, and right shoulder pain. Chest X-ray revealed homogeneous opacity at the lung apex and destruction of the first rib. Which of the following is not compressed?
explanation:
The given case scenario and chest X-ray features are suggestive of a tumor at the apex of the right lung, also called Pancoast tumor.

question_text: Which of the following structures passes through the foramen marked by the arrow?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The foramen indicated by the arrow is the aortic hiatus, situated at the level of the T12 vertebra.
  • Through this opening, the descending thoracic aorta continues as the abdominal aorta.
  • The thoracic duct also traverses this hiatus, carrying lymph from the lower limbs, abdomen, pelvis, and left upper body to drain into the left subclavian vein.
  • Additionally, the azygos vein may pass through this opening.
  • Unlike the esophageal and caval openings, the aortic hiatus lies behind the diaphragm rather than piercing it.

Diaphragmatic openings and vertebral levels:

  • Inferior vena cava (IVC) - T8: Passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm with the right phrenic nerve.
  • Esophagus - T10: Pierces the right crus of the diaphragm, accompanied by the vagus nerves.
  • Aorta - T12: Located at the aortic hiatus, transmitting the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein.

Explanation of other options:

Esophagus (Option A): Crosses the diaphragm at T10, not T12.

Inferior vena cava (Option B): Passes through the diaphragm at T8 to open into the right atrium.

Sympathetic trunk (Option D): Runs along the vertebral column and enters the abdomen through smaller gaps in the diaphragm, not via the aortic hiatus.

question_text: The arch of the azygos vein is derived from:
explanation:
The azygos system of veins are indirect descendants of the posterior cardinal veins, although arch of the azygos is old right posterior cardinal. The point at which azygos arch empties into superior vena cava in the adult marks the junction of old anterior cardinal above with old common cardinal below.

question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect for the marked structure?
option_a: It has a beaded appearance due to many valves
option_b: It enters the thorax through the vena caval opening of the diaphragm
option_c: It ends by opening into the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular vein
option_d: It ascends through the posterior mediastinum crossing from right to left

Explanation:

The marked structure is the thoracic duct. The thoracic duct does not enter the thorax through the vena caval opening. Instead, it enters the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm at the T12 level, along with the aorta and azygos vein.

Thoracic Duct Features:

  • Begins at the cisterna chyli (L1/L2)
  • Enters thorax via aortic hiatus (T12)
  • Ascends in posterior mediastinum between aorta and azygos vein
  • Crosses from right to left at T4-T6 levels (Option D)
  • Terminates at the left venous angle (junction of left subclavian + left internal jugular vein) (Option C)
  • Appears beaded due to the presence of multiple valves (Option A)

Key takeaways:

question_text: While viewing an exploratory surgery on a patient injured in an automobile accident, you see the surgeon elevate the esophagus off the vertebral bodies and look in the area between the azygos vein and descending aorta. What structure was she most likely looking for?
explanation:
The thoracic duct lies in the posterior mediastinum between the aorta on its left and the azygos vein on its right. These three structures are all found posterior to the esophagus. The greater thoracic splanchnic nerve lies anterior to the vertebral bodies, behind the azygos, thoracic duct, and aorta. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is found in the middle mediastinum, looping under the aortic arch before it ascends to the larynx. The right pulmonary artery is also in the middle mediastinum--it leaves the heart and enters the root of the right lung. The sympathetic trunk lies on the heads of the ribs on the posterior wall of the thorax.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 162

question_text: In superior or inferior vena cava obstruction, blood returns via the dilated azygos vein. Which adjacent structure running between the azygos vein and descending aorta is most likely to be compressed?
explanation:
Below the level of the sternal angle, the thoracic duct lies posterior to the esophagus, between the azygos vein and the descending aorta. So, if the azygos vein became dilated, it could impinge on the thoracic duct. The trachea is superior to the azygos vein, which loops over the right bronchus before emptying into the superior vena cava. This means that a dilated azygos vein would have little impact on the trachea. Because the azygos is on the right side of the body, it could not compress anything at the root of the left lung. The right phrenic nerve is anterior to the azygos vein. The descending aorta is much larger and more muscular than the azygos vein, so it is unlikely that it would be compressed by this much smaller structure.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 206

question_text: The structure marked in the image drains into:
option_a: Junction of superior vena cava and left brachiocephalic veins
option_b: Junction of left jugular and left subclavian veins
explanation:
Explanation :

The structure marked is the thoracic duct, which empties into the left venous angle-also known as the left jugulo-subclavian venous junction (angle).

Thoracic Duct

  • Principal lymphatic trunk, transporting chyle and most lymphinto the bloodstream.
  • Drains the entire body exceptthe right side of the head and neck, right upper limb, right lung, right thoracic wall, right heart, and convex surface of the liver.
  • Origin:Cisterna chyli at the level of T12.
  • Course:
    • Enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm.
    • Ascends in the posterior mediastinum, posterior to the esophagus.
    • At T5, deviates to the left and continues into the superior mediastinum.
  • Termination:At C7, empties into the left venous angle (junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins which together form the left brachiocephalic vein.

question_text: All of the following are contents of the posterior mediastinum except:
explanation:
Explanation:

The thymus is located in the superior mediastinum (and partly anterior mediastinum in children), not in the posterior mediastinum.

Posterior Mediastinum:

Boundaries:

  • Anteriorly: Pericardium, bifurcation of trachea, pulmonary vessels,
  • Posteriorly: Lower eight thoracic vertebrae and Intervertebral disc
  • On each side: Mediastinal pleura

Contents of Posterior Mediastinum:

  • Thoracic aorta
  • Oesophagus (Option B)
  • Azygos and hemiazygos veins (Option A)
  • Thoracic duct (Option C)
  • Vagus nerves and oesophageal plexus
  • Splanchnic nerves (greater, lesser, least)
  • Posterior mediastinal lymph nodes

Contents NOT found in Posterior Mediastinum:

  • Thymus (superior/anterior mediastinum)
  • Heart and pericardium (middle mediastinum)

question_text: All of the following nerves are present within the superior mediastinum except:
explanation:
Explanation:

The splanchnic nerves (greater, lesser, least) do not lie in the superior mediastinum. They originate from thoracic sympathetic ganglia and pass inferiorly through the posterior mediastinum to enter the abdomen.

Superior Mediastinum:

The mediastinum is the middle space left in the thoracic cavity in between the lungs.

The superior mediastinum is separated from the inferior by an imaginary plane by passing through the Sternal angle (anteriorly) and lower border of T4 vertebra (posteriorly).

Boundaries:

  • Anteriorly: Manubrium sterni
  • Posteriorly: Upper four thoracic vertebrae
  • Superiorly: Plane of thoracic inlet
  • Inferiorly: Imaginary plane
  • On each side: Mediastinal pleura

Nerves Present in the Superior Mediastinum:

  • Phrenic nerves (right and left) (Option A)
    • Descend anterior to the root of lungs.
  • Vagus nerves (right and left) (Option B)
    • Give branches including cardiac branches.
  • Left recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option C)
    • Branches from left vagus, loops under aortic arch (ligamentum arteriosum) and ascends.

Not in Superior Mediastinum:

  • Splanchnic nerves
    • Located in posterior mediastinum, running along vertebral bodies.

question_text: Which vessel courses across the mediastinum in an almost horizontal fashion?
explanation:
The left brachiocephalic vein joins with the right brachiocephalic vein to form the superior vena cava on the right side of the body. So, the left brachiocephalic vein must course across the mediastinum to reach its destination. The left subclavian artery and vein are lateral to the mediastinum, while the left jugular and common carotid travel vertically.

Reference-Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 128

question_text: You are attending an operation to remove a thymic tumor from the superior mediastinum. The surgeon asks, "What important nerve lying on and partly curving posteriorly around the arch of the aorta should we be careful of as we remove this mass? " You quickly answer, "The --
explanation:
The left vagus nerve lies against the lateral surface of the arch of the aorta. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is an especially important nerve from the vagus which loops around the aortic arch. This nerve innervates the muscles of the left larynx. If it is damaged, a patient may experience hoarseness after surgery. Care must be taken to preserve this nerve, especially during thyroid surgery.

The left and right phrenic nerves, which innervate the diaphragm, are lateral to the vagus nerves and are not looping near the aortic arch. The left and right sympathetic trunks lie on the posterior chest wall and are not involved with the aortic arch.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 231

question_text: Azygos vein drains into:
explanation: The azygos vein ends by joining the posterior aspect of the superior vena cava The Azygos Vein The azygos vein connects the superior and inferior venae cavae, either directly by joining the IVC or indirectly by the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins. The azygos vein drains blood from the posterior walls of the thorax and abdomen. It ascends in the posterior mediastinum It is covered anteriorly by the oesophagus as it passes posterior to the root of the right lung. It then arches over the superior aspect of this root to join the SVC. In addition to the posterior intercostal veins, the azygos vein communicates with the vertebral venous plexuses. This vein also receives the mediastinal, oesophageal, and bronchial veins.

question_text: Which of the following veins drains into the left brachiocephalic vein but not into the right brachiocephalic vein?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The left superior intercostal vein drains the 2nd to 4th intercostal spaces and empties specifically into the left brachiocephalic vein.
  • On the right side, the superior intercostal vein drains into the azygos vein, not the right brachiocephalic vein.

Thoracic Venous Drainage Patterns:

  • Left superior intercostal vein: Drains into the left brachiocephalic vein.
  • Right superior intercostal vein: Drains into the azygos vein.
  • Inferior thyroid veins: Usually drain into both brachiocephalic veins. (Option B)
  • Vertebral veins: Drain into both brachiocephalic veins. (Option A)
  • 1st posterior intercostal veins: Often drain into both brachiocephalic veins depending on the side. (Option C)

question_text: An 8-year-old boy is found to have a mid-line tumor of the thymus gland that is impinging posteriorly on a blood vessel. The affected vessel is most likely the:
explanation:
Remember that the ascending aorta is the short part of the aorta emerging from the heart before the aortic arch. The left brachiocephalic vein is the only vein listed which is anterosuperior to that part of the aorta. It crosses horizontally through the mediastinum to join with the right brachiocephalic vein and form the superior vena cava. The right brachiocephalic vein stays on the right side of the chest and would not be affected by the aortic aneurysm. The azygos vein is also on the right side of the chest, and it lays deep in the thoracic cavity. The internal thoracic vein lies on the interior surface of the anterior wall of the chest. Although it drains into the brachiocephalic vein, it would not be affected by the aneurysm. The left superior intercostal vein crosses the aortic arch laterally, but its blockage would only affect drainage of intercostal spaces 2-4 on the left side.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 127

question_text: At which vertebral level does the trachea bifurcate?
explanation:
The trachea bifurcates at the lower border of

T5 vertebra.

The trachea is 10 - 12 cm long and has 2 parts:

  • Upper cervical
  • Thoracic(in superior mediastinum)

In the mediastinum, at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra, the trachea divides into the right and left primary bronchi. The bronchi branch into smaller and smaller passageways until they terminate in tiny air sacs called alveoli.

question_text: In the development of the cardiovascular system:
option_a: Angiogenic clusters appear in the yolk sac endoderm
option_b: The midline heart tube forms four chambers
option_c: The aortic arches develop in a caudal to cephalic sequence
option_d: The heart begins to beat around the 21st day
explanation:
Angiogenic cell clusters appear in mesoderm only. The heart arises as two bilateral tubes that eventually fuse into one heart tube that begins to beat around the 21st day. When the aortic arches develop, they do so in a cephalic to caudal direction.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The myocardial layer of the heart tube develops from:
explanation:
Myocardium or heart muscle arises from the splanchnic mesoderm near the heart tubes in the cardiogenic region. Endocardium is also from this cardiogenic splanchnic mesoderm, from angiogenic cell clusters forming the heart tubes. Epicardium or visceral pericardium is from splanchnic mesoderm lining the intraembryonic coelom.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The epicardium forms from:
option_a: The epimyocardial layer of the heart
option_b: Dorsal mesocardium over the sinus venosus
explanation:
The epimyocardial layer of the developing heart develops from the splanchnic mesoderm between heart tubes and the intraembryonic coelom in the cardiogenic area. The part of the epimyocardium that lines this region of the coelom becomes visceral serous pericardium while mesoderm between this and the heart tubes becomes myocardium.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The blood vessels that carry relatively "pure" arterial blood during fetal development are:
explanation:
The posthepatic inferior vena cava carries oxygenated blood from the ductus venosus. Upon reaching the heart, most of this blood passes through the foramen ovale to the left heart and the ascending aorta, leaving poorly oxygenated blood entering from superior vena cava to reach right ventricle and pulmonary trunk

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The following are true statements with regard to the fetal circulation EXCEPT:
option_a: Since the fetal liver is a hemopoietic organ, it is large and well supplied with oxygenated blood
option_b: Fetal brain receives relatively pure arterial blood
option_c: Fetal and maternal blood vessels anastomose in the placenta
option_d: In early developmental stages, one pulmonary vein buds from the left atrium of the heart
explanation:
In the placenta, there is no anastomosis between the maternal and fetal vessels. Maternal blood from the spiral arteries enters the cotyledons, where it bathes the villi from the fetus. This all occurs without anastomosis.

question_text: The fetal right atrium is mainly derived from:
explanation:
The right sinus horn of the sinus venosus enlarges and forms the fetal right atrium. The left sinus horn regresses to form the main vein draining the heart muscle, the coronary sinus. The original right atrium becomes the right auricle and also part of right atrium anterior to the crista terminalis.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: The persistence of which of the following arch arteries is responsible for the congenital anomaly marked in the image given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The above marked defect is suggestive of Patent Ductus Arteriosus, which arises due to persistence of the 6th left pharyngeal arch artery.

Patent Ductus Arteriosus is a congenital heart defect where the ductus arteriosus - a fetal blood vessel that connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta fails to close after birth. Normally closes after birth due to decreased oxygen levels and decreased prostaglandin E2 (PGE2).

Explanation of other options:

6th right pharyngeal arch artery (Option B):

4th left pharyngeal arch artery(Option C):

The 4th left pharyngeal arch artery is crucial in forming the aortic arch, one of the major arteries carrying oxygenated blood from the heart to the body.

4th right pharyngeal arch artery (Option D): The 4th right pharyngeal arch artery is crucial in forming the Proximal part of the right subclavian artery.

question_text: Coronary sinus develops from ?
explanation: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Sinus venosus [Ref Essentials of human embryology p. 873] The Coronary sinus develops from the Sinus venosus segment of embryonic heart. Left horn of sinus venosus retrogresses to form part of coronary sinus

question_text: The aortic sac:
option_a: Is the area immediately distal to the ventricles
option_b: Is connected to the dorsal aorta via the aortic arch arteries
option_c: Is preserved as the region of the semilunar valves in the adult heart
option_d: Is also known as the truncus arteriosus
explanation:
The aortic sac receives blood from the truncus arteriosus and sends it into the aortic arch arteries which branch from it and connect it to the paired dorsal aortae. Aortic sac becomes the proximal part of aortic arch & the brachiocephalic trunk. Semilunar valves arise from the walls of truncus arteriosus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: From where the membranous part of the interventricular septum is derived from?
explanation:
The structure marked is the membranous part of the interventricular septum. It is derived from endocardial cushions.

Endocardial cushions are soft tissue masses that protrude in the atrioventricular and conotruncal regions.

  • Atrioventricular cushions are derived from overlying endocardial cells.
  • The conotruncal cushions are derived from the neural crest cells.

Endocardial cushions contribute to the formation of:

  • Atrial septa
  • Ventricular septa (membranous portion)
  • Atrioventricular canals
  • Atrioventricular valves
  • Aortic and pulmonary channels

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 171

question_text: Which of the following structures ruptures to create the transverse pericardial sinus?
explanation:
Early in heart development, the heart tubes are suspended within the intraembryonic coelom by the dorsal mesocardium. The rupture of this membrane and the folding of the heart tubes brings the outflow tract and inflow tract close together, producing the transverse pericardial sinus.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: In a patient with inferior vena caval obstruction, which of the following collaterals do not help drain the blood?
option_a: Superior epigastric and inferior epigastric vein
explanation:
Superficial epigastric and iliolumbar veins do not help to drain the blood in inferior vena cava

(IVC) obstruction as they drain into the IVC itself. Iliolumbar veins drain directly into the IVC and superficial epigastric vein drains via the femoral vein.

In IC obstruction, the collateral channels open up to drain the blood from the lower limb into the superior vena cava (SVC) and then to the heart.

The main collateral channels are via azygous and hemizygous veins and vertebral venous plexuses. They communicate with the common iliac veins by the ascending lumbar veins and tributaries of the inferior vena cava. Additionally, blood is also drained by inferior epigastric veins > superior epigastric veins > internal thoracic veins > brachiocephalic veins > superior vena cava.

Reference-Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 180

question_text: Which valves would be open during ventricular systole?
explanation:
Remember that ventricular systole is the period when the ventricles are contracting. This contraction forces blood out of the heart, which pushes the aortic and pulmonary valves open.

During systole, the tricuspid and mitral valves are closed. They are prevented from prolapsing (being pushed back into the atrium) by the chordae tendinae and papillary muscles

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 235

question_text: The Tetralogy of Fallot includes the following defects of the heart:
explanation:
The defects in the Tetralogy of Fallot are: pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. It results from abnormal conotruncal septation. Dexter, as in dextroposition, means right; sinster means left.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 164

question_text: Which of the following pairs is incorrect for cardiac valves and their auscultatory areas?
option_a: Pulmonary: 2nd left intercostal space near sternum
option_b: Aortic: 2nd right intercostal space near sternum
option_c: Mitral: 4th left intercostal space, 9 cm from sternum
option_d: Tricuspid: Right half of lower end of body of sternum
explanation:
Explanation:

The mitral valve is not auscultated at the 4th left intercostal space.

Its correct auscultation point is the: 5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line (approximately 9 cm from the sternum)

question_text: Cardiac tamponade is the condition that occurs due to:
explanation:
Explanation:

Cardiac tamponade occurs due to excessive accumulation of fluid in the pericardial cavity, which compresses the heart and restricts diastolic filling.
The most common cause is pericardial effusion, often secondary to pericarditis.

Pericarditis and Cardiac Tamponade

  • Pericarditis = inflammation of the serous pericardium
  • Leads to serous fluid accumulation in the pericardial cavity → pericardial effusion
  • When the fluid increases rapidly or excessively, it compresses the thin-walled atria, impairs ventricular filling, and reduces cardiac output
  • This life-threatening condition is called cardiac tamponade

Pericardiocentesis (Drainage of Pericardial Fluid)

Two common approaches:

  • Sternal approach:
    • Needle inserted in the left 5th or 6th intercostal space, close to the sternum
  • Subxiphoid approach:
    • Needle inserted at the left costo-xiphoid angle
    • Directed upward and backward at 45 degrees to the skin

Myocarditis (Option A):

  • Inflammation of the myocardium
  • Causes chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmias
  • Does not directly cause cardiac tamponade

Blockage of coronary arteries (Option B):

  • Produces myocardial ischemia and necrosis (heart attack)
  • Not a cause of tamponade

Angina pectoris (Option C):

  • Incomplete coronary obstruction, often due to vasospasm
  • Causes chest pain radiating to left arm
  • Not associated with pericardial fluid accumulation

question_text: The heart sound associated with the mitral valve is best heard:
option_b: In the second left intercostal space
option_c: In the second right intercostal space
option_d: In the fifth left intercostal space
explanation:
The four valves of the heart can be auscultated at very distinct spaces. The mitral valve can be ausculatated in the left 5th intercostal space, slightly below the nipple.The aortic valve can be ausculatated in the 2nd right intercostal space, just lateral to sternal angle. The pulmonary valve can be auscultated in the 2nd left intercostal space, just lateral to sternal angle. The tricuspid valve can be auscultated in the 4th left intercostal space, just lateral to sternum.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 201

question_text: The sound associated with tricuspid stenosis (narrowing) in a 40-year-old male would be best heard at which location on the anterior chest wall?
option_b: In the right 2nd intercostal space near the sternum
option_c: Over the apex of the heart
option_d: Xiphoid area, just off the sternum
explanation:
It's best to listen to sounds associated with the tricuspid valve at the fourth left intercostal space, just lateral to the sternum. The answer that comes the closest to this is E. What would you hear in the other spaces? Below the left nipple, in the fifth intercostal space, you would be auscultating the mitral valve. This is also the valve that you can hear at the apex of the heart. The right 2nd intercostal space near the sternum is the site for auscultating the aortic valve. Finally, it would be difficult to hear anything over the sternal angle, since the stethoscope would be over bone, which would blunt any sounds!

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 202

question_text: During a surgical procedure in the vicinity of the descending aorta, a surgeon accidentally cuts the first aortic intercostal arteries. Which of the following structures might be deprived of its main source of blood supply?
explanation:
The right bronchus receives blood from a single right bronchial artery. This artery may branch from one of the left bronchial arteries or it may branch from the right 3rd posterior intercostal artery, the first intercostal artery that arises from the descending aorta. Damaging this artery might stop the blood supply to the main bronchus. The intercostal arteries to the first and second intercostal spaces are derived from the highest intercostal artery, so the blood supply to either of these spaces would not be disrupted. The left bronchus is supplied by two left bronchial arteries which branch directly from the descending aorta. The fibrous pericardium is a fibrous sac that contains the pericardial cavity and the heart. Its blood supply is not a major concern.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 210

question_text: Which posterior mediastinal structure is most closely applied to the posterior surface of the pericardial sac?
explanation:
The esophagus is closely related to the posterior surface of the pericardial sac. After coming from the heart, the aorta arches over the left pulmonary artery and left bronchus. Eventually, just above the diaphragm, this vessel is posterior to the esophagus. The azygos vein, on the right side of the thorax, arches over the right pulmonary artery and bronchus. It is also posterior to the esophagus. The thoracic duct is posterior to the esophagus as well and does not contact the pericardial sac. Finally, the trachea is superior to the heart.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 217

question_text: In tricuspid atresia, there is usually:
option_d: All of the above are correct
explanation:
Tricuspid atresia:

  • In this condition, there is complete agenesis of tricuspid valves.
  • It is caused by an insufficient amount of tissue in AV cushion for the formation of tricuspid valve.
  • The tricuspid atresias are always associated with
    • Patent foramen ovale
    • VSD
    • Underdeveloped right ventricle
    • Hypertrophy of the right ventricle

question_text: The bulboventricular ridge of the embryonic heart:
option_a: Persists as the membranous part of the interventricular septum
option_b: Becomes the upper segment of the muscular interventricular septum
option_c: Contributes to the formation of the left atrioventricular orifice
explanation:
The bulboventricular ridge or flange initially separates the atrioventricular canal and primitive left ventricle from the bulbus cordis. However, it regresses, allowing communication between the primitive right and left ventricles. Ultimately, it vanishes.

question_text: The heart starts to beat in the week of development.
explanation:

question_text: In the development of the heart:
option_a: The coronary sinus is formed from the left horn of the sinus venosus
option_b: The oblique vein of the left atrium is formed from the left posterior cardinal vein
option_c: The valve of the coronary sinus is formed from the left sinus valve
option_d: The valve of the inferior vena cava is formed from the left sinus valve
explanation:
Left horn of sinus venosus forms coronary sinus and left common cardinal vein becomes oblique vein of the left atrium. The right sinus valve becomes the valve of the coronary sinus and the valve of inferior vena cava. Left sinus valve becomes part of interatrial septum.

question_text: The following features of the adult human body represent remnants of fetal circulation EXCEPT:
option_c: Oblique vein of the left atrium
explanation:
The pectinate muscles are merely small muscles on the inner surface of the atria. They are not remnants of the fetal circulation, as are the fossa ovalis, oblique vein, ligamentum arteriosum and ligamentum teres hepatis. Pectinate muscles are, however, remnants of the wall of the original atrium.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 185

question_text: The fetal left atrium is mainly derived from the:
explanation:
The primitive pulmonary vein becomes incorporated into the wall of the fetal left atrium, forming most of it. The original left atrium becomes a trabeculated atrial appendage called the left auricle, because it resembles an "ear" on the heart.

question_text: The least serious clinical problems can be expected from which of the following cardiac abnormalities?
explanation:
In the case of dextrocardia, there is transposition so that the heart and great vessels are mirror images of normal. This is a benign situation that is often accompanied by transposition of abdominal viscera, as well. As long as there are no other defects, the patient may never notice the abnormality.

Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, Cardiovascular System Embryology Page number - 170

question_text: All of the following form the boundaries of the Triangle of Koch except:
explanation:
Explanation:

The Triangle of Koch is an important anatomical landmark in the right atrium, containing the AV node. Its boundaries are:

  1. Tendon of Todaro
  2. Ostium of coronary sinus
  3. Septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve

The Crista terminalis is not a boundary. It is a vertical ridge in the right atrium separating the smooth sinus venarum from the rough pectinate muscle area.

Triangle of Koch
A crucial triangle used in electrophysiology and cardiac surgery to locate the AV node.

Boundaries:

  • Tendon of Todaro: Fibrous extension from the Eustachian valve to central fibrous body
  • Coronary sinus ostium: Posterior boundary
  • Septal cusp of tricuspid valve: Inferior boundary

Clinical relevance:

  • AV node lies at the apex of the triangle
  • Key landmark during ablations and valve surgeries
  • Avoids injury to conduction tissue

question_text: Which structure does NOT lie in the coronary sulcus?
explanation:
The coronary sulcus is the groove which separates the atria from the ventricles. The right and left coronary arteries, circumflex artery, and coronary sinus all lie in this groove. The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery which lies on the right ventricle and supplies that chamber of the heart.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 206

question_text: Boundary of the Koch's triangle is not formed by?
explanation: Koch's Triangle is a triangle enclosed by the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve, the coronary sinus, and the membranous part of the interatrial septum. Koch’s triangle: Walter Karl Koch (1880–1962) was a distinguished German surgeon who discovered a triangular-shaped area in the right atrium of the heart that marks the atrioventricular node (known as Koch's triangle). The three sides of the triangle are defined by the following structures within the right atrium: The ostium of the coronary sinus, posteriorly; The anterior portion of the tricuspid valve annulus; and The tendon of Todaro (a tendinous structure connecting the valve of the inferior vena cava ostium to the central fibrous body), posteriorly. Importance: Used as an anatomical landmark for location of the atrioventricular node during electrophysiology procedures such as pacing or ablation.

question_text: Which statement is true of the right atrioventricular valve?
option_a: It is also called the mitral valve
option_b: It is open during ventricular diastole
option_d: It is opened by the pull of chordae tendineae
explanation:
Ventricular diastole is the period when the ventricles relax and fill with blood. So, the AV valves need to be open at this time so that blood can flow from the atria to the ventricles. The right AV valve is called the tricuspid valve--it has three leaflets. The left AV valve is called the mitral valve and has two leaflets. Remember, the right side of the heart is pumping blood to the lungs so that it can be oxygenated. So, the blood flowing through the right AV valve will be deoxygenated, while the blood flowing through the left AV valve will be oxygenated. Finally, remember that the chordae tendineae and the papillary muscles do not pull the AV valves open! These structures serve to prevent the valves from prolapsing during systole.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 201

question_text: In JVP, the "a" wave represents?
option_c: Tricuspid valve bulging into the right atrium
explanation:
Explanation:

The "a" wave occurs due to right atrial contraction, which increases pressure in the right atrium and produces a positive deflection in the JVP.

This corresponds to the end of diastole (just before ventricular systole).

Prominent 'a' wave is seen in tricuspid stenosis and Pulmonary hypertension


Key Takeaways:

  • The "a" wave in the JVP represents right atrial contraction.
  • The "x" descent follows the "a" wave and represents atrial relaxation.
  • The "c" wave is caused by the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the atrium during early ventricular systole.
  • The "v" wave represents right atrial filling after ventricular systole.

question_text: The given finding is associated with?
explanation:
Explanation:

Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) results from the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21. Individuals often present with characteristic facial features, intellectual disability, and various medical complications. One hallmark feature is a single transverse palmar crease (simian crease), observed in about half of those affected, making this the correct association.

Aetiology:

  • Caused by meiotic nondisjunction in maternal or paternal gametes.
  • Occurs in approximately 1 in 800-1000 live births.
  • Overexpression of genes on chromosome 21 leads to the clinical phenotype.

Key Clinical Features:

  • General: Intellectual disability, flat facial profile, upward-slanting eyes with epicanthic folds, small nose with flattened bridge, narrow palate, small teeth, furrowed protruding tongue, hypotonia, small brachycephalic skull, dysplastic ears.
  • Hands and Feet: Short, broad hands, clinodactyly of the fifth finger, simian crease, sandal gap between the first and second toes.

Comorbidities:

  • Heart: 40-60% have congenital heart disease (AVSD, VSD, ASD, PDA, TOF).
  • GI: 12% have atresias (e.g., duodenal), increased risk of annular pancreas, and Hirschsprung disease.
  • Eyes: Risk of cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, decreased visual acuity.
  • Hearing: 40-60% have conductive hearing loss; routine assessment recommended.
  • Thyroid: Hypothyroidism in 13-54%.
  • Skeletal: Atlanto-occipital instability in 10-30%; monitor with lateral neck X-ray.
  • Growth: Slower linear growth; potential obesity; hypotonia improves with age.
  • Malignancy: Increased risk of leukemia and transient lymphoproliferative syndrome.
  • Neurology: Early-onset Alzheimer's due to APP gene on chromosome 21.

Explanation of other options:

question_text: Blockage of blood flow in the proximal part of the anterior interventricular artery could deprive a large area of heart tissue of blood supply, unless a substantial retrograde flow into this artery develops via an important anastomosis with which other artery?

question_text: While attempting to suture the distal end of a coronary bypass onto the anterior interventricular artery, the surgeon accidentally passed the needle through the adjacent vein. Which vein was damaged?

Then, you need to identify the vein that also lies in the anterior interventricular sulcus. And that vein is the great cardiac vein. The anterior cardiac vein lies on the surface of the right atrium--it drains directly into the right atrium. The coronary sinus is located in the coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus--it is formed by the union of the great cardiac vein and the oblique vein of the left atrium, and it drains blood directly into the right atrium. The middle cardiac vein is located in the posterior interventricular sulcus--it accompanies the posterior interventricular artery. question_text: A 40-year-old female presents with sudden onset chest pain and shortness of breath. Auscultation reveals absent breath sounds over the left lung, and chest X-ray confirms a pleural effusion. What is the most preferred site for pleural tap (thoracocentesis)?

explanation:
Explanation:

The preferred site for pleural tap is the 6th, 7th, or 8th intercostal space in the midaxillary line, with the 6th ICS midaxillary being the most commonly used safe entry point.

  • It avoids injury to the lung (above the 6th ICS lung margin drops).
  • It avoids the diaphragm (which begins rising at 8th ICS).
  • Best access to the costodiaphragmatic recess where fluid collects.

Always insert just above the upper border of the rib to avoid intercostal vessels and nerve.

Pleural Tap (Thoracocentesis):

  • Done to remove pleural fluid for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes.
  • Fluid gravitates to the costodiaphragmatic recess, best reached in midaxillary line.

Surface Anatomy Recall:

  • Lung lower border in midaxillary line: 8th rib
  • Parietal pleura lower border: 10th rib
  • Safe zone for tapping: between 6th-8th ICS, midaxillary.

1st ICS midaxillary line (Option A): Too high; lung apex occupies this area. Risk of pneumothorax.

2nd ICS anterior axillary line (Option B): Used for emergency needle decompression, not pleural effusion drainage.

4th ICS anterior axillary line (Option C): Still too high; fluid accumulates lower in the thorax.

Pulmonary trunk

  • The pulmonary trunk originates from the upper part of the right ventricle (infundibulum) near the sternal end of the third left costal cartilage.
  • It measures about 5 cm in length.
  • Course: It arises in the middle mediastinum, travels upward, backward, and to the left, and ends just below the aortic arch in front of the left principal bronchus.
  • At its termination, it divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

question_text: Which statement is true about the right lung?
option_a: It is slightly smaller than the left lung
option_b: It has a lingular segmental bronchus
option_c: It occupies the rightmost portion of the mediastinum
option_d: Its upper lobar bronchus lies behind and above the right pulmonary artery
explanation:
The structures at the root of the lung have different relationships in the right and left lungs. On both sides, the pulmonary veins are anterior and inferior while the bronchus is posterior. The difference between the two sides involves the pulmonary arteries. On the right side, the arteries are anterior to the bronchus, while on the left side the arteries are superior to the bronchus. The right lung is slightly larger than the left lung, and the lingula is found in the left lung only. Neither lung is in the mediastinum--the mediastinum is the space between the two pleural sacs. Finally, the phrenic nerve passes anterior to the root of the lung--on both the left and right sides.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 128

question_text: The lowest extent of the pleural cavity, into which lung tissue does not extend, is known as the:
explanation:
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the area inferior to the lung where the costal and diaphragmatic pleura are continuous. This is the lowest extent of the pleural cavity. The costomediastinal recess is a small anterior recess where the costal and mediastinal pleura are continuous. The cupola is the pleural space that extends above the first rib. The inferior mediastinum is a term sometimes used to refer to the anterior, middle, and posterior subdivisons of the mediastinum all together. The pulmonary ligament is a fold of pleura located beneath the root of the lung.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 162

question_text: A frail, elderly man, suspected of having widespread cancer of the lungs and bronchi, is brought in for bronchoscopic examination. The instrument is inserted into the airway, where it accidentally punctures the thin, brittle posterior wall of the diseased right main bronchus. A sudden gush of blood immediately indicates that the instrument has also torn the wall of the blood vessel immediately behind the right main bronchus, i.e., the:
explanation:
The azygos vein lies immediately behind the right mainstem bronchus. This vein then arches over the right mainstem bronchus to drain blood into the superior vena cava. So, this must be the structure that was damaged during the bronchoscopy.The left brachiocephalic artery doesn't exist, but the brachiocephalic trunk is a branch off the aortic arch which travels far superior to the area of interest. The pericardiacophrenic artery is a branch of the internal thoracic artery which accompanies the phrenic nerve. It is anterior to the right bronchus. The right pulmonary veins are inferior and anterior to the right mainstem bronchus. Finally, the superior vena cava is superior and anterior to the right mainstem bronchus. 

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 162

question_text: The minor (horizontal) fissure separates:
option_a: The lower lobe from the lingula
option_b: The upper lobe from the lingula
option_c: The lower lobe from both the middle and upper lobes
option_d: The middle lobe from the upper lobe
explanation:
The horizontal fissure cuts across the right lung in such a way as to separate the middle lobe from the upper lobe. The oblique fissure separates the lower lobe from both the middle and upper lobes. Remember that the lingula is only on the left lung, and it is part of the superior lobe.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct for bronchopulmonary segments except:
option_a: It is aerated by secondary lobar bronchi
option_b: It is anatomical, functional and surgical sector of lung
option_d: There are 10 segments in each lung
explanation:
Explanation:

Bronchopulmonary segments are not aerated by secondary (lobar) bronchi. They are supplied by tertiary (segmental) bronchi.

Bronchopulmonary Segment Features:

  • Basic anatomical, functional, and surgical unit of the lung (Option B)
  • Each segment is supplied by a tertiary (segmental) bronchus
  • Each segment receives a branch of the pulmonary artery
  • Veins lie in the intersegmental septa, separating segments
  • It is a bronchovascular segment because each has its own bronchus + artery (Option C)
  • Number of segments: (Option D)
    • Right lung: 10 segments
    • Left lung: Usually 8-10 segments (some fuse)

Key takeaways:

Bronchopulmonary segments are 10 pyramid-shaped functional lung units, each supplied by a segmental bronchus and artery, with veins located between segments.

question_text: A 4-year-old girl is brought in with coughing, and you are told by her mother that she had been playing with some beads and had apparently aspirated one (gotten it into her airway). Where would you expect it to most likely be?
explanation:
There are several reasons why inhaled objects will be more likely to enter the right lung instead of the left lung. First, the carina, a ridge-like structure at the bifurcation of the trachea, is set a little towards the left. So, there is a more direct path for objects to fall to the right. Also, the right bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical than the left bronchus. All of these factors mean that an inhaled object will enter the right main bronchus. It would be almost impossible for a bead to get lodged in the terminal bronchiole of the right lung - that is a very small space!

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 127

question_text: In a post-soccer match brawl, a 35-year-old man was stabbed in the back with a knife that just nicked his left lung halfway between its apex and diaphragmatic surface. Which part of the lung was most likely injured?
explanation:
Because of the sharp angle of the oblique fissure, the posterior surface of the left lung is almost entirely comprised of the inferior lobe. So, a stab wound halfway between the apex and diaphragmatic surface of the lung would result in injury to the inferior lobe. The hilum is the point at which the structures forming the root of the lung enter the lung. The lingula is part of the superior lobe, which forms the anterior and superior sides of the lung. And remember, the middle lobe isn't relevant here because it is on the right lung. (Besides, it doesn't even contribute to the posterior surface of the right lung.)

Reference-Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Thorax, Page number - 127

question_text: Bronchopulmonary segments are aerated by which of the following bronchi?

question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding the bronchopulmonary segment?
option_a: It is drained by independent intrasegmental branch of pulmonary vein
option_b: It is the largest subdivision of a lobe
option_c: It is named according to the segmental bronchus supplying it
explanation:
The bronchopulmonary segments are not drained by an independent branch of the pulmonary vein.

The tributaries of the pulmonary vein tend to pass intersegmentally between and around the margins of segments.

A bronchopulmonary segment is the area of lung supplied by a segmental bronchus and its accompanying pulmonary artery branch.
